textClarifications.title: Crossing a Boundary
textClarifications.original:
When a wave enters a new medium, its frequency stays the same because the source hasn’t changed. However, the speed and wavelength usually change to match the properties of the new material.




For example, when a wave moves from air into water, it might slow down and its wavelength gets shorter, but the number of cycles per second (frequency) remains constant. This is why waves can look and behave differently after crossing a boundary.
textClarifications.revised:
At a boundary, a wave can enter a medium where its speed is different. The frequency stays fixed by the source, so the wavelength changes with the speed.

For example, light entering water from air slows down, so its wavelength becomes shorter. Other wave types can behave differently: sound travels faster in water than in air. Always identify the wave and the two media.

textClarifications.title: Decibel Scale
textClarifications.original:
Loudness is measured in decibels (dB). Normal conversation is about 60 dB, while a rock concert can reach 120 dB.




Sounds above 120 dB can be painful or even cause hearing damage.
textClarifications.revised:
Sound intensity level is measured in decibels (dB), a logarithmic scale. An increase of 10 dB represents ten times the sound intensity; an increase of 20 dB represents one hundred times the intensity.

Intensity is a physical quantity. Perceived loudness also depends on the listener and the frequency of the sound.

textClarifications.title: Open and Closed Pipes
textClarifications.original:
Instruments like flutes (open pipes) and clarinets (closed pipes) have different patterns of nodes and antinodes. This changes which notes and harmonics they can produce.




Open pipes have antinodes at both ends, while closed pipes have a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end.
textClarifications.revised:
In the ideal open-open air column, both ends are displacement antinodes: air particles can move most freely there. Its lowest-frequency mode has a displacement node at the center.

In an ideal closed-open column, the closed end is a displacement node and the open end is a displacement antinode. Its lowest mode fits one quarter of a wavelength in the tube. Pressure nodes and antinodes occur at the opposite locations.

textClarifications.title: Beside Source
textClarifications.original:
If you are directly beside the moving source, you hear the true frequency the source emits. The wavefronts are neither compressed nor stretched in your direction.




This means there is no Doppler shift for observers positioned exactly to the side of the moving source.
textClarifications.revised:
The sound heard now was emitted earlier. The Doppler shift depends on the source motion along the line from its position at emission to the observer.

In the classical model, motion perpendicular to that line at emission gives no frequency shift for a stationary observer. Simply standing beside the source at the moment of reception does not guarantee zero shift, because sound takes time to travel.

textClarifications.title: Mach 1 and the Mach Cone
textClarifications.original:
When the object reaches Mach 1—the speed of sound—it moves as fast as the waves it creates. The overlapping wavefronts form a cone-shaped shock wave called a Mach cone.




The angle of the cone depends on how much faster than sound the object is moving.
textClarifications.revised:
Mach number compares the source speed with the sound speed in the surrounding medium. Mach 1 means those speeds are equal.

Above Mach 1, the source outruns its sound waves. The wavefronts form an envelope called a Mach cone, trailing behind the source. The cone becomes narrower as the Mach number increases.

textClarifications.title: Shock Wave and Sonic Boom
textClarifications.original:
The shock wave created by the Mach cone spreads outward and eventually reaches the ground. When it passes by an observer, it is heard as a sudden, loud sonic boom.




This boom is the result of all the compressed sound energy being released at once.
textClarifications.revised:
A supersonic source produces a shock wave: a thin region where pressure changes rapidly. An observer hears a sonic boom when this pressure disturbance passes.

The boom is not all the sound energy being released at once. The source continues to produce the shock pattern while it travels supersonically.

textClarifications.title: Refraction
textClarifications.original:
Refraction is the bending of light as it passes from one material into another with a different density. For example, a straw looks bent in a glass of water because light changes direction at the water’s surface.




This effect is not just a visual trick—it’s a fundamental property of how light interacts with materials.
textClarifications.revised:
Refraction is a change in a wave’s direction as it enters a medium where its speed differs. For light crossing a boundary at an angle, a change in refractive index usually bends the ray.

For example, light entering water from air slows and bends toward the normal. The normal is perpendicular to the surface. A ray entering straight along the normal changes speed but does not bend.

textClarifications.title: Refractive Index
textClarifications.original:
The refractive index is a number that tells us how much light slows down and bends in a particular material. The higher the refractive index, the more the light will bend.




For example, glass has a higher refractive index than air, so light bends more when entering glass from air.
textClarifications.revised:
Refractive index compares the speed of light in vacuum with its speed in a material: n = c/v. A higher refractive index means light travels more slowly in that material.

For the same starting medium and angle of incidence, entering a material with a higher refractive index bends the ray closer to the normal. Refractive index, rather than mass density alone, determines this behavior.

textClarifications.title: Speed of Light in Different Materials
textClarifications.original:
Light travels fastest in a vacuum, a bit slower in air, and even slower in water or glass. This change in speed is what causes light to bend at the boundary.




The greater the difference in speed between the two materials, the more the light will change direction.
textClarifications.revised:
Light travels fastest in vacuum, at approximately 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s. It travels more slowly in materials such as water and glass.

At a boundary, the frequency stays the same, while speed and wavelength can change. A ray crossing at an angle can change direction; a ray entering along the normal does not bend.

textClarifications.title: Short Wavelength, High Frequency
textClarifications.original:
Waves with short wavelengths and high frequencies, like microwaves, can carry lots of data quickly. This makes them ideal for technologies like Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, which need to transfer large amounts of information in a short time.




However, these waves don’t travel very far and can be easily blocked by walls or other obstacles. That’s why your Wi-Fi signal might drop when you move to another room.
textClarifications.revised:
Shorter-wavelength electromagnetic waves have higher frequencies. Many higher-frequency communication bands offer wide available bandwidth, which can support high data rates.

Carrier frequency alone does not determine data rate. Usable bandwidth, signal-to-noise ratio, and the communication design matter. Obstructions and atmospheric absorption can also limit a link.

textClarifications.title: Long Wavelength, Low Frequency
textClarifications.original:
Waves with long wavelengths and low frequencies, such as radio waves, can travel much farther and pass through obstacles more easily. This is why AM radio signals can be received from stations hundreds of kilometers away.




These waves, however, can’t carry as much data as higher-frequency waves. They’re better for simple signals, like voice or basic music broadcasts.
textClarifications.revised:
Longer-wavelength electromagnetic waves have lower frequencies. They often diffract more noticeably around obstacles of a given size, and some bands support long-distance propagation.

Range is not determined by wavelength alone. Transmitter power, antennas, terrain, noise, and atmospheric conditions also matter. A lower carrier frequency does not automatically mean a lower data rate.

textClarifications.title: Choosing the Right Wave
textClarifications.original:
Engineers select the frequency and wavelength based on what the technology needs. For example, Wi-Fi uses higher frequencies for fast data transfer over short distances, while radio uses lower frequencies for long-range communication.




This careful selection helps balance speed, range, and reliability, ensuring each technology works best for its purpose.
textClarifications.revised:
Choose a frequency band by considering the whole communication link: required range, obstacles, available bandwidth, antennas, power, and noise.

A higher carrier frequency can offer access to wider bandwidth, but frequency alone does not set data rate. The best choice balances capacity and reliable coverage for the intended use.

textClarifications.title: Frequency and Wavelength
textClarifications.original:
The frequency and wavelength of a signal determine how much data it can carry and how far it can travel. Higher frequencies can transmit more information but usually have a shorter range.




Lower frequencies travel farther and penetrate obstacles better, but they can’t carry as much data at once. Engineers choose frequencies based on the needs of each wireless system.
textClarifications.revised:
Frequency and wavelength are related by c = fλ for electromagnetic waves in vacuum, approximately also in air. Higher frequency means shorter wavelength.

Wavelength affects diffraction and antenna design. Available bandwidth and signal-to-noise ratio help determine data capacity; carrier frequency alone does not. Range also depends on power, antennas, obstacles, and the environment.

textClarifications.title: Uncontrolled Fission
textClarifications.original:
Uncontrolled fission occurs when there is nothing to absorb or slow down the neutrons, causing the reaction to accelerate rapidly. This results in a massive, explosive release of energy.




Uncontrolled fission is the principle behind nuclear weapons, where the goal is to release as much energy as possible in a very short time.
textClarifications.revised:
A chain reaction grows when each fission leads, on average, to more than one additional fission. The number of fissions then increases from one generation to the next.

Control depends on the neutron balance: some neutrons cause further fissions, while others escape or are absorbed. The diagram compares a growing chain with a steady chain; slowing neutrons and absorbing neutrons are different processes.
